entries.name: Claude Agent SDK for TypeScript
entries.reason: Anthropic presents the Python and TypeScript libraries as language bindings for one Claude Agent SDK product; the Atlas represents that product through the canonical Python repository rather than duplicating the same operational system.
entries.useful_lesson: Language bindings can differ in implementation visibility and license terms even when they expose one product boundary.

entries.name: Google ADK for Go
entries.reason: Google presents Go, Python, TypeScript, Java, and Kotlin implementations as one Agent Development Kit; the Atlas represents the product through the canonical Python repository rather than scoring language bindings separately.
entries.useful_lesson: Cross-language framework parity, test-support licensing, and provider integration depth should be reviewed without multiplying product records.

entries.name: LangSmith
entries.reason: The reviewed repository is a client SDK for tracing and evaluation; it does not itself provide a memory system or a tool-acting agent runtime.
entries.useful_lesson: Agent tracing, evaluation, production observability, and recovery-oriented operations.

entries.name: SQL Chat
entries.reason: The reviewed implementation is a chat-based SQL client that generates and executes user-selected statements, but it does not own an iterative planning, validation, or repair loop required by the data-analysis agent role.
entries.useful_lesson: Conversational database UX, locally stored connection data, self-hosting, and explicit query execution.

entries.name: Gorgias Cortex
entries.reason: Gorgias describes Cortex as its flagship internal AI agent for Gorgias employees rather than a deployable or directly purchasable system available to Atlas users. The public Gorgias AI Agent is a separate customer-facing ecommerce product and is not substituted for Cortex.
entries.useful_lesson: Internal agents can demonstrate cross-application work, employee adoption, and operational patterns without establishing a public product boundary.

entries.name: Hugging Face Text Generation Inference
entries.reason: The repository is archived, so the runtime no longer represents an operational choice a reader could adopt. Hugging Face Inference Endpoints remains separately represented as a managed inference service, and that service boundary is not substituted for the archived runtime.
entries.useful_lesson: Production serving engines can reach end of life while the managed service built on them continues; collection boundaries should be checked against repository lifecycle, not brand continuity.

entries.name: llamafile
entries.reason: llamafile packages llama.cpp and model weights into one portable executable. Its own documentation states it relies on llama.cpp for serving and inherits that project's server interface and endpoints, and the repository pins the upstream commit rather than forking it. What it adds is a distribution format, not a separate execution boundary, so the published llama.cpp record already represents the runtime. No local-runtime type fits it either: it manages no model store, and nothing embeds it because it embeds the weights.
entries.useful_lesson: A packaging innovation can be genuinely valuable without being a distinct operational boundary; check whether the candidate serves models itself or delegates to a runtime already represented.

entries.name: Unify
entries.reason: Unify's routing product was retired and the successor was retired in turn; its console states the product is no longer available, and its pricing and documentation pages return not-found. A service a reader cannot sign up for is not an operational choice, matching the treatment of archived runtimes.
entries.useful_lesson: A routing aggregator can disappear faster than the models it routes to, so a dated check of the operator's own console is worth more than a live marketing page.

entries.name: ModelScope API-Inference
entries.reason: ModelScope operates a genuine first-party inference API rather than proxying another platform, so the duplication concern does not apply. It is excluded because its own documentation declares the service non-commercial and not for profit, tells developers not to use it for tasks needing concurrency or service-level guarantees, and refers commercial demand to other platforms. Access is metered by community credits that are earned rather than bought, and no billing exists. The directory curates operated services with commercial commitments.
entries.useful_lesson: Check the reason a service is excluded, not just the conclusion: the expected ground here was duplication of a sibling platform, and that turned out to be false while a different disqualification was stated plainly in the vendor's own limits page.

entries.name: Superpowers
entries.reason: The repository describes itself as a software development methodology built on composable skills, and it ships no agent machinery: the package declares no executable and no dependencies, and its session hook only reads a skill document and prints it as additional context. Its subagent workflow is prose instructing a host agent to call the host's own tools, so nothing runs when the host harness is removed. CURATION.md keeps prompt templates and collections as research inputs rather than operational systems.
entries.useful_lesson: Adoption does not establish an operational boundary: at 280,000 stars this was the most-starred candidate in the sweep and still resolves to documentation that a host agent executes.

entries.name: STORM
entries.reason: The reviewed repository is a paper implementation rather than an operational system. Its readme presents a research preview and states the system cannot produce publication-ready articles; it ships no tests at all, its only continuous integration is a formatting check, its package still declares alpha status, its last substantive code change predates this review by more than a year, and it hard-pins a two-year-old version of the framework its own documentation calls its core. Nothing here distinguishes its outcome from a published research agent either.
entries.useful_lesson: A laboratory release can be genuine executable code with real entry points and still be a research input. The tell is not whether code exists but whether any correctness gate does, and whether the dependency floor is frozen at the paper's date.

entries.name: Stagehand
entries.reason: The current major version removed its agent loop on purpose. Its own migration guide states the built-in orchestrator is gone and that the library now exposes discrete tools and leaves the control flow to the caller, so it no longer owns the iterative browse-act-observe workflow the browser-agent role requires. It is a driver library that hands a browser to some other agent as tools, and the Atlas has no role for tool providers; classifying it as a framework would describe the brand rather than the operational product.
entries.useful_lesson: A vendor can turn an agent into a library by deleting the loop. Re-read the migration notes of a major version before trusting the role a candidate held one version earlier.

entries.name: Agent S
entries.reason: The reviewed repository is paper code for three successive papers rather than an operational system. The library exposes a single-step prediction call and leaves the loop to a fifteen-step demo command line that executes model-generated Python on the host directly beneath a comment promising a confirmation prompt that does not exist. It carries one provider-configuration test, a formatting-only continuous-integration check, no package development-status classifier, no release since December 2025, and keeps four paper versions with their benchmark harnesses side by side. The vendor's maintained product is a separate proprietary cloud desktop agent.
entries.useful_lesson: A company-published paper implementation can be maintained enough to merge community provider changes and still lack any correctness gate. The additional tell here is that the loop lives in the demo, not the library.

entries.name: herdr
entries.reason: The system owns terminals rather than agents. Its package manifest describes it as a terminal workspace manager for coding agents, and its documentation says it does not wrap or replace them but owns their terminals. It makes no model calls and holds no identity, memory, skills, or schedules of its own; the agent state it shows is inferred by pattern-matching the screen text of another product. It is well built, and it is a process supervisor.
entries.useful_lesson: A tagline promising the runtime your agents live on can mean a process supervisor. Check for a provider directory before checking for a memory directory.

entries.name: deep-research
entries.reason: The repository is a deliberately minimal reference implementation rather than an operational system. Its readme sets a goal of staying under five hundred lines, its research step is a fixed recursion over one search vendor in which the model never selects a tool, and it ships no test runner, no continuous integration, and no release; the last code change predates this review by more than a year, and its package manifest declares a different licence from its licence file.
entries.useful_lesson: A recursion with a model at each step is not a tool loop. Check whether the model can choose an action or only fill a slot in a pipeline the caller parameterised.

entries.name: InsForge
entries.reason: A relational backend-as-a-service for coding agents whose ten products are database, authentication, storage, realtime, functions, a model gateway, sites, messaging, payments, and compute. Its one memory route is three commits old, undocumented, and not exposed through its tool server, and a vector extension inside a general database offering is not retrieval infrastructure any more than it is in the hosted database platforms it compares itself to. The agent is the operator of the backend, not the subject it serves.
entries.useful_lesson: Vector and embedding topics on a repository identify a database extension, not a memory system. Check the products page before the schema.

entries.name: MiroThinker
entries.reason: The repository is a model release with an evaluation harness rather than an operational agent. Its readme is a model card of weight collections, parameter tables, and benchmark charts, and its quick start frames the bundled scaffold as what it recommends running those weights with. It has no tests: the test configuration declares a test directory and a full coverage and type-checking stack, and no such directory exists anywhere in the tree. Its only workflow is a lint and format check. It has no tags, no releases, and neither of its packages exists on a package index. Its single entry point hard-codes an example task, all fifteen of its scripts are benchmark evaluation runners, and the benchmark tree sits inside the agent application. The maintained framework is a separate repository the readme never links, and the operational product the readme markets is a proprietary hosted agent.
entries.useful_lesson: A large orchestrator with rollback and turn budgets can still be a research input. The tell is not the sophistication of the loop but whether the repository is something a reader installs: here the test configuration points at a directory that was never written, which is a sharper signal than the absence of tests alone.

entries.name: claude-squad
entries.reason: The system owns terminals rather than agents, on the same grounds as a previously excluded terminal workspace manager. It makes no model calls at all: its dependency manifest names no provider client and no HTTP client, and a search of its source for provider endpoints returns nothing. Its persisted model is a flat list of terminal sessions with no task, run, order, or message entity, and the agent state it displays is inferred by matching prompt strings in another product's screen output. The only occurrences of the word handoff in the tree are a help-screen heading for commands that hand work back to the human.
entries.useful_lesson: A handoff heading in a help screen can name the handoff to the human. Check whether the persisted schema has a second entity beside the session before believing an orchestrator is there.
